summary.text: Rail transport moves people and goods on wheeled vehicles running along tracks, usually two parallel steel rails.
Modern rail began with the steam locomotive in the United Kingdom at the start of the 19th century, and the first passenger railway, the Stockton and Darlington, opened in 1825.
Railways spread quickly through Europe and North America, lowering shipping costs and creating national markets where prices varied less from city to city.

facts.label: Global share
facts.value: About 8% of passenger and freight transport

facts.label: First passenger railway
facts.value: Stockton and Darlington Railway, opened in 1825

facts.label: US transcontinental trip
facts.value: Days instead of months, at one-tenth the cost

facts.label: Oldest operational railway
facts.value: Middleton Railway in Leeds, built in 1758, excluding funiculars

items.prompt: Why can rail cars be hitched into much longer trains than a line of trucks on roads?

options.label: Rail cars are lighter than trucks, so engines can pull more of them
Rolling stock on rails meets lower frictional resistance than road vehicles
Rail cars are always pulled by electric engines that never tire
Roads wear out whenever vehicles are linked together

items.explain: Rolling stock on rails generally meets lower frictional resistance than rubber-tyred road vehicles, so rail cars can be coupled into longer trains.

items.prompt: After rail arrives, a merchant notices the price of the same goods in distant cities growing closer together. What explains it?

options.label: Rail made goods cheaper to make in every city
Governments set the same price in each city
Rail cut shipping costs, creating national markets
Wagons carried goods faster than trains did

items.explain: Rail lowered shipping costs compared with water or wagon, which led to national markets where prices varied less from city to city.

items.prompt: A rancher in the American West cannot turn a profit because shipping is too costly and rivers are few. What changed that?

options.label: Railroads brought cheap, economical transport
New rivers opened to shipping across the region
Stagecoach lines ran more often
Aeroplanes carried the cattle to market

items.explain: Economical transportation by rail meant farming, ranching and mining could be done at a profit in the West, which had few navigable rivers.

items.prompt: Why has rail had a revival in recent decades after losing ground to cars and aeroplanes?

options.label: Rail became more flexible than road transport
New steam locomotives replaced diesel ones
Cars and aeroplanes became too slow to compete
Road congestion, rising fuel prices and government efforts to cut CO₂

items.explain: Rail revived due to road congestion and rising fuel prices, as well as governments investing in rail to reduce CO₂ emissions.

items.prompt: Horse-hauled wagonways with wooden rails first appeared in the 1550s. What job were they built for?

options.label: Moving passengers between cities
Hauling boats across a narrow strip of land
Delivering mail to distant towns
Carrying ore tubs to and from mines

items.explain: Wagonways using wooden rails and hauled by horses started appearing in the 1550s to carry ore tubs to and from mines.

items.prompt: A company must deliver to many scattered small towns on short notice. Why might rail be the weaker choice?

options.label: Rail is less flexible than road transport
Rail cannot carry heavy loads
Rail is less energy efficient than trucks
Rail cannot be coupled into long trains

items.explain: Railway transport is capital-intensive and less flexible than road transport, though it carries heavy loads with greater energy efficiency and safety.

paragraphs.heading: What a railway is
paragraphs.text: A railway carries people and goods in wheeled vehicles that run on tracks, usually two parallel steel rails. Along with roads, it is one of the two main ways to travel over land. Wheels on rails meet less friction than rubber tyres on a road, so many cars can be coupled into one long train, usually pulled today by a diesel or electric locomotive. Railways cost a lot to build and are less flexible than roads, but they move heavy loads more safely and with less energy.

paragraphs.heading: Long before steam
paragraphs.text: Railways moved by people or animals go back to the ancient world. In Greece, a paved trackway called the Diolkos carried boats across the Isthmus of Corinth from around 600 BC and stayed in use for more than 650 years. From the 1550s, wagonways with wooden rails and horse-drawn carts began hauling ore to and from mines, and they soon caught on across Europe. In one such mine, pictured in Germany in 1556, the miners called their carts Hunde, or dogs, after the noise they made on the tracks.

paragraphs.heading: Steam takes over
paragraphs.text: Modern rail began when the steam locomotive was invented in the United Kingdom early in the 19th century. The Stockton and Darlington Railway, the first passenger line, opened in 1825, and the first link between two cities opened in England in 1830. After that, railways spread quickly across Europe and North America and became a key part of the Industrial Revolution.

paragraphs.heading: Faster and far cheaper
paragraphs.text: Railways made moving goods quicker and much cheaper than shipping by water or wagon. Prices began to differ less from one city to the next, forming what are called national markets. In the United States, the first transcontinental railroad let people and freight cross the country in days rather than months, at a tenth of the cost of a stagecoach or wagon. Cheap transport made farming, ranching and mining pay in the West, a region with few rivers boats could use, and the railroads transformed the country.

paragraphs.heading: After the steam age
paragraphs.text: Railways kept changing. Electrification began in the 1880s with tramways and rapid transit lines, and from the 1940s diesel locomotives replaced steam. Japan opened the first high-speed rail system in 1964, and such lines now link many cities across Europe, East Asia and the eastern US. After losing ground to cars and planes, rail has revived in recent decades thanks to crowded roads, rising fuel prices, and governments backing it to cut CO₂ emissions.
